description: Test your knowledge of MI8.{1-2,4} | Genitourinary & Sexually Transmitted Infections.

cards.text: What is the most common route of UTI infection and which organisms typically cause it?
cards.answer: Ascending route (>95% of UTIs): faecal bacteria colonize perineum, ascend urethra to bladder, ureter, and kidney. Most commonly caused by E. coli.

cards.text: What is the key virulence factor of E. coli that causes pyelonephritis?
cards.answer: P fimbriae (pili), which bind blood group P antigen on renal tubular cells, enabling colonization of the renal parenchyma.

cards.text: Why are women more prone to uncomplicated UTI than men?
cards.answer: Short urethra (4 cm vs 20 cm), proximity of urethral meatus to anus, and mechanical introduction of bacteria during sexual intercourse.

tip.tip: Women: shorter tube = easier bacterial ascent

cards.text: What is CAUTI and what is the associated bacteriuria risk per day of catheterization?
cards.answer: Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) is the most common hospital-acquired infection with 3-7% daily risk of bacteriuria due to biofilm formation on catheters.

cards.text: What is the diagnostic threshold for significant bacteriuria in a mid-stream clean-catch (MSU) specimen?
cards.answer: ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism is considered significant bacteriuria in MSU specimens.

cards.text: How does Proteus mirabilis contribute to stone formation in complicated UTI?
cards.answer: Proteus produces urease enzyme, which alkalinizes urine, leading to precipitation of struvite and magnesium ammonium phosphate stones.

tip.tip: Proteus urease → alkaline urine → struvite stones

cards.text: Why must asymptomatic bacteriuria be treated in pregnant women?
cards.answer: Progesterone-induced ureteral dilatation and mechanical obstruction cause urinary stasis; asymptomatic bacteriuria progresses to pyelonephritis in 20-40% of untreated pregnant women.

tip.tip: Pregnancy stasis = 20-40% progression risk if untreated

cards.text: What is the gold standard specimen collection method when contamination is a concern, and why?
cards.answer: Suprapubic aspiration (SPA): a sterile procedure where ANY bacterial growth is significant. Used in infants and equivocal cases because contamination is impossible.

tip.tip: SPA = sterile puncture; ANY growth = positive
